title: Why three? A two-level system with four mutually unbiased questions
abstract: Two sharp yes/no questions are mutually unbiased if and only if their involutions anticommute. A set of unbiased questions is therefore a Clifford algebra, whose maximal size is odd, meaning four anticommuting questions typically imply a fifth: the two-level systems of real, complex and quaternionic quantum theory allow two, three and five questions, while four is skipped. Without this operator product restriction, a two-level system with four unbiased questions exists as the four-dimensional Bloch ball, the hyperbit. The single-system postulates that pick out the Jordan state spaces allow such a model, and only energy observability rules it out. We show what it lacks, and realise it inside two qubits: its Kirkwood-Dirac imaginary parts are hidden $\mathfrak{so}(4)$ generators, its composites allow entanglement but no interaction, and its 24-cell of states stays Spekkens preparation contextual down to depolarising strength $2/3$. In fermionic terms, the four questions are the Majorana operators of two modes while the fifth is parity: the four-question system is therefore the sector removed by parity superselection.
summary: This paper explores the theoretical limits of quantum measurement by examining systems supporting four mutually unbiased questions (the hyperbit), contrasting it with the standard qubit. It shows that while the hyperbit can be mathematically constructed, it fails to satisfy several key physical postulates (like generating dynamics) that the qubit possesses. The work uses advanced tools from algebra and quantum information theory to delineate the boundaries between different quantum models.
main_problem: The paper investigates the maximum number of mutually unbiased questions (MUBs) a two-level system can support, contrasting the standard result of three with the theoretical possibility of four.
main_result: While standard operator algebra restricts MUBs to an odd number (2, 3, or 5), a hypothetical 'hyperbit' with four MUBs can be constructed, but it lacks key physical properties like dynamics generation and algebraic closure compared to a standard qubit.
method: The analysis combines algebraic constraints (Clifford algebras, anticommuting involutions) with geometric modeling (Bloch balls, 24-cell) and quantum information diagnostics (contextuality proofs, Kirkwood-Dirac distributions).
model_or_system: The primary models are the standard qubit (two-level system) and the hypothetical hyperbit (a four-level system), which is shown to embed into a two-qubit system.
key_observables: Mutually Unbiased Questions (MUBs), Clifford algebra structure, preparation contextuality (measured via inequalities), and the imaginary part of the Kirkwood-Dirac correlation function.
important_parameters: The number of MUBs ($n=2, 3, 4, 5$), the dimension of the state space (Bloch ball dimension), and the contextuality threshold ($\lambda > 2/3$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often assumes preparation noncontextuality when deriving bounds on correlations, and it compares the hyperbit against the full set of single-system postulates.
figures_summary: TABLE I compares four key properties (A-D) across systems with $n=2, 3, 4, 5$, illustrating the structural differences between the qubit and the hyperbit.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the algebraic constraints on MUBs, then introduces the geometric model of the hyperbit, compares its properties to the qubit using diagnostic criteria, and finally analyzes its embedding and contextuality within a two-qubit framework.
why_interesting: It provides a deep theoretical exploration of the limits of quantum measurement theory, extending the concept of MUBs beyond standard qubit models and linking algebraic structure to physical realizability.
